# `silk/simd/simd`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

Facts about SIMD vectors on the target CPU of the current compilation.

## When to use
Use [`preferredBytes`](#preferredBytes) with `static if` to pick a vector width for a kernel, and
[`hardware`](#hardware) to fall back to scalar code where vectors would only be emulated. Use the
per-shape modules such as `silk.simd.u8x16` for the vector operations themselves.

## Details
The answers come from the CPU model and features of the compilation profile, the same facts
that `Target.hasCpuFeature` reads. They do not depend on the host machine and have no runtime
cost.

## Examples
### Pick a block width for a kernel
```silk
import silk.simd.simd

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let width = simd.preferredBytes()
  if width != 16 && width != 32 && width != 64 {
    return 1
  }
  return 0
}
```

Import as `simd` with `import silk.simd.simd as simd`.

Public declarations: 2.

<a id="preferredBytes"></a>

## `preferredBytes`

```silk
pub static fn preferredBytes() -> usize
```

Returns the vector width, in bytes, that the target CPU handles best.

### Details

The width is `64` when AVX-512BW is enabled, `32` when AVX2 is enabled, and `16` otherwise,
including on AArch64 and wasm32. Vectors of any admitted width still compile on every target.

<a id="hardware"></a>

## `hardware`

```silk
pub static fn hardware() -> bool
```

Returns `true` if the target CPU executes 128-bit vectors in hardware.

### Details

This is always `true` on x86-64 and AArch64. On wasm32 it is `true` only with the `simd128`
feature; without it, vector operations compile to scalar code.
